analysis.one_liner: Requires lobbyists to disclose who funded the research they submit to federal rulemakers, and creates a public advocate to help ordinary people shape federal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Oversight committees in December 2021, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in November 2022, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies write the detailed rules that implement laws — on air quality, workplace safety, drugs, and finance — and companies try to shape those rules by flooding agencies with comments and studies. This bill would require anyone submitting scientific or economic research in a rulemaking to disclose who paid for it, whether an interested party reviewed or edited it, and any financial ties to the researchers, and would make those studies public. It would also create an Office of the Public Advocate to help ordinary people navigate and participate in rulemaking, let citizens sue to enforce rules (with a share of any penalty as a bounty), fine public companies that submit knowingly false material to agencies, bar regulated industries from the formal 'negotiated rulemaking' process, codify courts' duty to defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous laws, and require agencies to respond to petitions with 100,000 signatures.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who comment on federal rules but lack paid lobbyists: they would get a public advocate office to help them participate, automatic notification of proposed rules, guaranteed responses to petitions with 100,000 signatures, and public disclosure of who funded the research behind the rules that affect them. Public-interest groups also gain a citizen-suit tool with financial rewards to enforce rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people, consumers, and public-interest groups

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone submitting scientific, economic, or technical research in a rulemaking comment to disclose who funded it, whether an affected party reviewed or revised it, and any financial relationship with the researcher — and makes the underlying studies public.
Requires public disclosure when a submitted study draws 10% or more of its funding from an entity the agency regulates, or when such an entity exercised editorial control over the research.

Creates an Office of the Public Advocate in the Office of Government Ethics to help individuals participate in rulemaking, respond to petitions, and reach communities historically excluded from the process, in multiple languages.
Lets private citizens sue to enforce federal rules or the bill's own disclosure requirements and recover 15–30% of the proceeds, modeled on False Claims Act whistleblower suits.
Codifies courts' duty to defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of ambiguous statutes, and requires agencies to explain withdrawn rules and disclose changes made during White House review.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and trade associations that currently submit industry-funded studies and mass comments to shape rules without disclosure, and public companies that would face fines starting at $250,000 for submitting knowingly false information to agencies. Federal agencies and the White House regulatory review office (OIRA) would face new procedural obligations and litigation exposure.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new private right of action letting anyone sue to enforce rules — or challenge an agency's failure to follow its own procedures — with whistleblower-style bounties of 15–30% of proceeds. Critics across the political spectrum warn this could invite barrages of litigation against agencies and regulated parties, potentially chilling the very rulemaking the bill aims to strengthen.

Codifying Chevron deference in statute cuts both ways: it protects expert agencies from being second-guessed by courts, but it also locks in deference to whichever administration controls the agencies, reducing judicial checking of agency interpretation regardless of who is in power.

Restricting negotiated rulemaking to governments and limiting OIRA's early communications would restructure a process that, whatever its flaws, currently lets regulated industries, unions, and public-interest groups shape complex rules before they are proposed — some legal scholars argued the change could slow the rules agencies do issue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to the public — transparency about who funded the research behind federal rules, a public advocate to help people navigate agencies, whistleblower-style enforcement, and statutory protection for agency expertise — are real but hard to quantify, and they come with honest costs: a private right of action against rule violations could flood courts with litigation, forcing agencies to defend routine rules and potentially slowing or scaring agencies off protective rulemaking altogether; and codifying judicial deference removes a check that critics of agency overreach value. On balance the design leans toward the public, but the enforcement mechanism is aggressive enough that reasonable people could object to its scale.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee after referral, was sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, and never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
Eleven months later, on November 1, 2022, it was referred to the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote on the bill appears in its action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill never gained cosponsors beyond the 12 House Democrats who signed on at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and trade groups that influence federal rules by submitting industry-funded studies and mass public comments; their methods faced no new disclosure requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies whose funded research faced no disclosure

sides.party_line_note: All 13 initial supporters (sponsor plus 12 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and the bill advanced no further in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.industry: Corporate lobbyists and law firms that dominate rulemaking comments
industries.note: Funding-disclosure and public-study requirements would expose anonymous, industry-funded research used to influence agency rules, weakening a core lobbying tool. The bill was introduced in response to the practice of 'junk science' and shell groups filing mass public comments.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations regulated by federal agencies
industries.note: The bill imposes fines starting at $250,000 (doubling per repeat violation) on public companies that submit knowingly false material to agencies in rulemaking, and requires them to attach their prior annual report to comments.

Agencies gain statutory protection for their interpretations of ambiguous law and face outside pressure to issue rules on time, but they also lose the negotiated-rulemaking and early-OIRA-review flexibility some agencies rely on and face citizen suits for procedural missteps.

industries.industry: OIRA / White House regulatory review apparatus
industries.note: The bill keeps OIRA's review role but time-limits it to 45–90 days, bans pre-submission meetings, and forces disclosure of changes made during review — reforming rather than abolishing the channel through which regulated interests influence rules.
